storm.summary_layperson: Radar shows strong thunderstorm cells 17–38 miles to the north, but they're tracking away from the cove for now — the bigger story tonight is that the atmosphere itself stays primed for new storms to fire through the evening, and any that do develop won't get the Sound's usual protective boost after the marine layer fades around 9:20 PM.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Marine layer holds a strong 11°F air-water gap at 6 PM, fading to about 4°F by 10 PM as the air cools faster than the Sound — the protective buffer is effectively gone by roughly 9:21 PM, though nothing is currently tracking toward the cove to test it.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows a cluster of strong cells (up to 54 dBZ) 17–38 miles north to northwest of the cove, but the tracked motion has them moving away (NNW at roughly 20 kt) rather than closing — none of the five nearest cells shows a positive closing speed toward Greenwich right now.

That doesn't make the evening low-risk: the atmosphere itself is primed, with CAPE of 2,770 J/kg and 24 kt of bulk shear (WSW), an environment the NWS Area Forecast Discussion specifically calls out for an "iso-sct pulse strong to severe threat in the high CAPE weak shear environment" this evening. New cells can fire on short notice in this setup even with the current complex retreating.

The cove's usual defense — the Long Island Sound marine layer — is present but on the clock. Water sits at 73°F against 84°F air, an 11°F gap right now, but as the air cools after sunset (8:04 PM) while the Sound holds steady, that gap narrows below the ~5°F protective threshold by about 9:21 PM. Anything that develops and tracks toward the cove before then would likely get slowed or weakened crossing the Sound; anything after that time would arrive at closer to full strength.

Regionally, only an Air Quality Alert and a Heat Advisory are active — no severe thunderstorm or tornado warnings at this time. If a new cell organizes and closes to within 25 miles at ≥45 dBZ, or a warning is issued, risk would escalate to high.

wind.tactics_blurb: SSW sea breeze reinforced by a light onshore gradient — expect it to hold past the 8:04 PM sunset rather than collapsing outright, easing to drifter conditions by the end of the window. Pressure is fairly even across the cove; play the oscillations rather than committing hard to one side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Both ingredients for a sea breeze are in place: an 11.2°F air–water temperature gap (well above the 5°F gate) and a synoptic gradient that's onshore (SW, forecast ~9 mph) and light enough to reinforce rather than oppose the thermal. Regionally, 71% of coastal stations are reading southerly against 0% of inland stations — the classic sea-breeze signature — while the open-water/airport ensemble reads a stronger 9.0 kt than the sheltered cove itself. That combination makes this a sea-breeze-reinforced-by-gradient day: expect it to hold roughly 30–60 minutes past the normal sunset collapse because the gradient flow persists after the thermal itself fades.

HRRR's raw surface direction (S, 177°) is running about 19° behind the real sea breeze — western-LIS stations are already at SSW (196°). The fetcher's maturation correction adds 15° of veer, putting the corrected forecast at SSW (192°); that's the direction used for the 18:00–19:00 rows above. After the thermal fades near sunset, the remaining flow reverts toward the raw HRRR gradient direction (SSW, 194–212°).

Cove geography: SSW–SW flow runs cleanly up the cove's N–S axis with only slight channeling along the west shore, so pressure should stay fairly even across the course — no strong lean to either side tonight.

Shift character: expect a persistent right-veering shift through 18:00 as the sea breeze finishes maturing, settling into normal 10–20° oscillations by 19:00. After sunset the wind eases and direction may wander a bit more as gradient flow alone takes over.

On the water: RYC is currently reading SSE at 5.1 kt gusting 8.4 — sheltered and light compared to the open-water 9 kt gradient, typical for this cove. Expect 5–6 kt through the middle of the window (light-air range, finicky but raceable), easing to 3 kt by 22:00 as the thermal component is gone and only a light gradient remains. No postponement risk, but don't expect big breeze late.
